title: The Universe Has Some Truly Weird Galaxies. Euclid Is Photographing Them by the Millions
content:
The universe is a strange place, filled with delightfully bizarre structures. Some galaxies look like enormous glowing eyes. Others are being torn apart by their neighbors. Some appear stretched into rings and arcs by gravity itself.

Now, a European space telescope is photographing these cosmic oddities by the millions.

The European Space Agency unveiled observations of more than 900 million galaxies captured by its Euclid telescope. But the spectacular pictures are just a bonus. Euclid has a much bigger mission: building the largest three-dimensional map of the universe ever made, and using it to investigate two of cosmology’s greatest mysteries — dark matter and dark energy.

A telescope with a very big job

Launched in July 2023, Euclid operates around 1.5 million kilometers (930,000 miles) from Earth, near a gravitationally stable region called the second Sun–Earth Lagrange point. In Lagrange points, the telescope is almost in perfect gravitational balance between the Sun and Earth, so it doesn’t have to spend much fuel.

It’s from that vantage point that Euclid is investigating dark matter and dark energy.

Dark matter is invisible material whose gravity helps hold galaxies together and shapes the universe’s large-scale structure. Dark energy is the mysterious phenomenon associated with the accelerating expansion of space.

Together, they account for roughly 95% of the universe’s total matter-energy content. The Earth, the Sun, all the stars and all the matter we can detect is just 5%. The other two mysterious things, whatever they are, make up the bulk of the universe.

We can see them doing things, but scientists still don’t know what they really are. Good luck sorting this out, Euclid.

×

The approach of this mission is to survey billions of galaxies across more than a third of the sky, looking back through approximately 10 billion years of cosmic history.

Euclid also analyzes the light coming from galaxies to estimate how far away they are. By combining distance measurements with their positions in the sky, astronomers can reconstruct the universe in three dimensions, mapping the enormous filaments and clusters that make up the cosmic web.

The latest release provides the building blocks for that map.

As it turns out, those building blocks are also some of the coolest space photos we’ve ever seen.

The galaxy that looks like an eye

One particularly striking object is NGC 1291, a galaxy that looks almost uncannily like an enormous eye staring back at us.

A brilliant center is surrounded by a hazy disc and an outer ring of stars. Tiny blue patches reveal “stellar nurseries,” regions where new stars are forming.

But why the ring?

Galaxies aren’t rigid objects. Their stars orbit under the influence of gravity, and structures such as central bars can redistribute material and create ring-shaped concentrations of stars and gas.

The result can be a remarkably orderly structure emerging from the complicated motion of billions of stars.

Elsewhere, Euclid has captured galaxies that look considerably less peaceful.

When galaxies get too close

Galaxies might look peaceful from afar, but their interactions can be spectacularly violent.

Consider Messier 81, a magnificent spiral galaxy roughly 12 million light-years away. Its gravity influences neighboring galaxies, including the smaller NGC 3077, distorting their structures and helping trigger new episodes of star formation.

Nearby, Euclid also photographed Holmberg IX, a small, irregular collection of blue stars.

Unlike a grand spiral, Holmberg IX has no majestic arms or obvious central bulge. Gravitational interactions involving Messier 81 and Messier 82 may have helped ignite its star formation.

Another of Euclid’s targets, NGC 1316, bears spectacular streams of stars produced by interactions with smaller galactic companions.

These stellar streams are essentially cosmic archaeological evidence. Long after galaxies interact, the displaced stars preserve traces of what happened.

Sometimes, galaxies only look distorted

Some of the strangest shapes in Euclid’s images aren’t really the shapes of galaxies at all.

They’re optical illusions created by gravity.

Einstein predicted that massive objects could bend the path of light traveling through space. When a distant galaxy happens to sit behind a sufficiently massive foreground galaxy, its light can be stretched into luminous arcs, distorted images, or even nearly perfect circles called Einstein rings. This phenomenon is called a gravitational lens.

Euclid’s latest dataset contains approximately 15,000 candidates for strong gravitational lenses.

That’s an extraordinary haul for a phenomenon once considered exceptionally rare.

And these distortions are scientifically valuable. By measuring how light bends, astronomers can estimate the total mass of the foreground galaxy, including the dark matter that cannot be seen directly.

Zooming out on large swaths of the universe

Perhaps Euclid’s most impressive achievement is its ability to zoom between extraordinary scales.

One image captures the Horologium supercluster, a gigantic assembly of more than 30 galaxy clusters roughly 800 million light-years away. The panorama also contains far more distant galaxies whose light has traveled billions of years to reach us.

In another view, two galaxy clusters appear to overlap, despite being separated by approximately five billion light-years. It’s a striking reminder that a two-dimensional photograph can conceal enormous distances.

That’s precisely why Euclid’s three-dimensional map matters.

The mission will reveal how galaxies congregate, how their enormous cosmic structures have changed over billions of years, and how dark matter and dark energy have shaped that evolution.

And this is only the beginning.

The November release covers roughly 14% of Euclid’s planned survey area.

The biggest map of everything

Euclid is still near the beginning of its scientific journey. The latest release provides only the foundation for its eventual three-dimensional map. More observations and analyses will allow scientists to reconstruct how the universe’s vast structures developed over billions of years.

But the progress is slow and steady.

The ultimate goal is to understand how invisible dark matter helped assemble those structures, and how dark energy has influenced their evolution.

For now, we get to enjoy an extraordinary preview. We get to see striking galaxies, bizarre phenomena, and some regions of space that look almost impossible.

But each one is another clue to how the universe became what it is today.
